There is a thick black line between the black dot and the small gray circle, representing the spring displacement direction or target direction; the velocity arrow v points roughly upward from the black dot, and the included angle α is marked between it and the thick black line. Reasoning: Take the direction of the thick black line as the reference meridian. The launch kinetic energy is K, so the initial velocity v0 = sqrt(2K/m). For the meridian trajectory with α=0, when reaching near the cylinder, the available kinetic energy according to the route given in the problem is Kc = K - mgR(1 - cos θ0) + (1/2)mgR θ0 sin θ0. If the launch angle is relatively small, the transverse initial velocity component is v0 sin α ≈ v0 α. When just grazing the cylinder of radius r, b = r. Therefore αmax = r/(R sin θ0) sqrt(Kc/K). Substituting Kc gives αmax = r/(R sin θ0) sqrt(1 - [mgR(1 - cos θ0) - (1/2)mgR θ0 sin θ0]/K).

A cylinder of radius $r \ll R \theta_{0}$ is placed on top of the sphere. Suppose the mass is launched at an angle $\alpha$ away from the direction of the spring's displacement with kinetic energy $K$, as shown.

What is the maximum angle $\alpha_{\max}$ at which the mass can be launched such that it can still hit the cylinder? Express your answer in terms of $K, m, g, \theta_{0}, r$, and $R$. You may assume $K$ is large enough for the mass to reach the cylinder for $\alpha=0$.

method.method_draft: Forward impact-parameter route. First read the top-view diagram: the large gray disk is the sphere seen from above, the small gray disk is the cylinder target, the black dot is the mass, the thick segment from the mass toward the cylinder is the spring-displacement direction, and the velocity arrow is launched at angle α from that segment. Take that segment as the reference meridian. From the text, use cylinder radius r with r << R theta0 and launch kinetic energy K. Compute the launch speed v0 = sqrt(2K/m). For the meridional α = 0 trajectory, use work-energy from the launch point to the cylinder: the kinetic energy available near the cylinder is Kc = K - m g R(1 - cos theta0) + (1/2) m g R theta0 sin theta0. The transverse launch component is v0 sin α ≈ v0 α. Use conservation of azimuthal angular momentum, or equivalently conservation of transverse impact parameter in the small-angle limit, to map this transverse component into a miss distance b = R sin(theta0) α sqrt(K/Kc). The mass just hits the cylinder when b = r. Solving gives αmax = r/(R sin theta0) sqrt(Kc/K) = r/(R sin theta0) sqrt(1 - [m g R(1 - cos theta0) - (1/2)m g R theta0 sin theta0]/K).

method.method_draft: Time-reversed acceptance-cone route. First read the diagram as a top view: the mass is the black dot, the cylinder target is the gray disk, the black segment gives the direct spring-displacement direction, and α is the angular aiming error of the velocity relative to that direct line. Instead of propagating a launched trajectory forward, reverse the motion: ask what narrow cone of trajectories leaving the cylinder backward would pass through the launch point. The cylinder radius r subtends a small transverse angular tolerance delta = r/(R sin theta0) in the top-view azimuthal direction. Compute the speed ratio between the cylinder point and the launch point by energy conservation along the direct path: v_c/v_0 = sqrt([K - m g R(1 - cos theta0) + (1/2)m g R theta0 sin theta0]/K). By time-reversal symmetry and conservation of the tangential/angular-momentum invariant, the launch-angle acceptance is the geometric tolerance multiplied by this speed ratio: αmax = delta (v_c/v_0). Substituting delta gives αmax = r/(R sin theta0) sqrt(1 - [m g R(1 - cos theta0) - (1/2)m g R theta0 sin theta0]/K).
